# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review

### Introduction and the Paradigm of Vascular Restoration
The treatment of obstructive coronary artery disease has evolved from plain old balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents (BMS) [1] and second-generation drug-eluting stents (DES) [2]. While contemporary metallic DES have dramatically reduced restenosis and target lesion failure (TLF), they leave a permanent metallic cage in the vessel wall. This "full-metal jacket" restricts the natural vasomotion of the coronary artery, risks late stent fracture, and serves as a substrate for chronic inflammation, neoatherosclerosis, and very late stent thrombosis [3]. 

To overcome these long-term limitations, the concept of bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS) was introduced. The paradigm of "vascular restoration" proposes that a temporary scaffold provides transient mechanical support and drug elution during the high-risk healing phase, subsequently resorbing to leave a natural, functional vessel [4]. Early-generation poly-L-lactide (PLLA)-based polymeric devices, such as the Absorb everolimus-eluting BVS (Abbott Vascular), showed early feasibility and safety in first-in-man clinical evaluations [5].

### First-Generation Scaffolds: Promise vs. Reality
The translation of this concept into large-scale randomized trials produced mixed results. The ABSORB II trial was the first to evaluate long-term vasomotion and late lumen loss, showing no significant difference in vasomotion at 3 years but revealing a higher rate of adverse events compared to metallic DES [6]. The pivotal, large-scale ABSORB III trial met its primary noninferiority endpoint for TLF at 1 year [7], but 3-year outcomes showed higher rates of target vessel myocardial infarction (TVMI) and scaffold thrombosis (ScT) with BVS [8]. These safety concerns persisted through the 5-year follow-up, representing the critical window of complete scaffold resorption [9]. Similar mid-term safety signals and increased rates of device-related events were reported in the ABSORB China [10] and ABSORB Japan [11] trials. 

To address these safety signals, the ABSORB IV trial was designed using optimized implantation techniques [12]. Although BVS achieved 1-year noninferiority, the long-term 5-year results of ABSORB IV still showed slightly higher rates of TLF with BVS, though the risk of very late scaffold thrombosis was attenuated [13]. Concurrently, the Amsterdam Investigator-Initiated Absorb Strategy All-Comers (AIDA) trial, which evaluated BVS in routine clinical practice, was terminated early by its data and safety monitoring board due to a higher-than-expected rate of ScT [14]. The final 5-year AIDA outcomes confirmed a persistent safety gap prior to complete device bioresorption [15]. 

These clinical findings were consolidated in pooled individual patient-data meta-analyses, which confirmed higher rates of TLF and device thrombosis with first-generation BVS compared with CoCr-EES at 2 years [16], 3 years [17], and 5 years of follow-up [18].

### Mechanistic Insights and Implantation Techniques
The suboptimal performance of first-generation BVS was driven by mechanical and procedural factors. Unlike thin-strut metallic DES, first-generation polymeric BVS required thick struts (~150 μm) to maintain adequate radial strength, which disrupted laminar blood flow, promoted rheological turbulence, and delayed endothelialization [19]. Mechanistic analyses of scaffold failures demonstrated that suboptimal lesion preparation, undersizing, and inadequate post-dilatation were primary triggers for acute and late ScT. Consequently, the "PSP" (Pre-dilate, Size properly, Post-dilate) technique was developed and clinically mandated to optimize scaffold expansion and apposition [20]. 

In response to these safety concerns, a joint task force of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and the European Association of Percutaneous Coronary Interventions (EAPCI) issued restrictive clinical guidance, recommending that first-generation BVS should not be used outside of clinical registries [21]. While some trials, such as the ABSORB TROFI II study in patients with ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), demonstrated favorable early vascular healing with BVS [22], the first-generation Absorb BVS was ultimately withdrawn from the commercial market.

### Next-Generation Scaffolds and Future Horizons
The commercial withdrawal of first-generation BVS spurred the development of next-generation devices with alternative materials, thinner struts, and optimized degradation profiles. Resorbable magnesium scaffolds (RMS), such as Magmaris (Biotronik), offered a metallic bioresorbable backbone with faster resorption kinetics (~12 months). The BIOSOLVE-II trial demonstrated the feasibility and safety of Magmaris in de novo coronary lesions [23], and its safety profile was maintained at 3-year pooled follow-up [24]. These findings were subsequently confirmed in the large, real-world BIOSOLVE-IV registry, which showed low rates of TLF and scaffold thrombosis [25].

Concurrently, novel polymer technologies emerged. The Fantom sirolimus-eluting scaffold (Reva Medical), constructed from an iodinated desaminotyrosine polycarbonate polymer, achieved thinner struts (125 μm), intrinsic radiopacity, and favorable 6-month clinical outcomes in the FANTOM II trial [26]. Thin-strut PLLA-based polymeric scaffolds also advanced, such as the 100 μm MeRes100 sirolimus-eluting scaffold, which showed favorable clinical and imaging results in the MeRes-1 trial [27]. Similarly, the NeoVas sirolimus-eluting scaffold demonstrated comparable clinical outcomes to CoCr-EES in randomized evaluations [28]. Furthermore, the ultra-thin (100–125 μm) Firesorb sirolimus-eluting BRS demonstrated excellent angiographic and safety profiles at 1 year in the FUTURE-II trial [29].

Importantly, BVS technology is finding unique niche applications beyond routine PCI. The PROSPECT ABSORB trial investigated the use of the Absorb BVS to treat angiographically non-obstructive, high-risk vulnerable plaques with large plaque burdens. At 25-month follow-up, preemptive stenting with BVS safely and significantly increased the minimum lumen area compared to medical therapy alone [30].

### Conclusion
Bioresorbable vascular scaffolds remain a highly attractive concept for percutaneous coronary intervention. Although first-generation devices suffered from thick struts and suboptimal deployment techniques, next-generation thin-strut polymeric and metallic scaffolds, paired with optimized implantation protocols, show great promise in overcoming past limitations and establishing a durable role in modern interventional cardiology.
